title: Same But Different & Which One Doesn’t Belong
subtitle: Two short comparison routines that build precise mathematical language and the habit of justifying a claim — one uses a pair, the other a set of four.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Sue Looney, Same But Different Math · Christopher Danielson, Which One Doesn’t Belong? · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: Two routines in the same family. Both ask students to **compare, then justify** — and both have no single right answer, so every student has a way in.

items: **Same But Different** shows *two* things and asks: how are they the *same*, and how are they *different*? It forces students to find shared structure *and* name a precise difference.

**Which One Doesn’t Belong? (WODB)** shows *four* things (a 2×2 set) and asks: which one doesn’t belong? Its design guarantee is that *every* one can be argued to not belong for some reason — so the debate, not the answer, is the point.

blocks.text: They’re close cousins. Use them as two formats of one move: **compare → justify → be precise.**

Choose **Same But Different** when you want students to surface *equivalence or the link between two representations* (1/2 vs 2/4; a table vs its graph) — the two-column “same / different” makes that crisp. Choose **WODB** when you want students to reason about *properties and attributes* (even/odd, prime, perfect square; four graphs; four shapes) — the “everything is defensible” set guarantees universal participation and rich argument.
What they develop

blocks.text: How each one runs
Same But Different (a pair)

items: Show the two things side by side
Silent think → turn-and-talk: “same… different…”
Record in two columns: *Same* | *Different*
Press for precision: “Same *how*, exactly?”
Name the big idea (equivalence, representation…)

blocks.text: WODB (a set of four)

items: Show the 2×2 set
Silent think → “which doesn’t belong, and why?”
Collect a reason for *each* of the four
Press for the math: name the property behind each reason
Celebrate that every one can be defended

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Precise claims naming a property (“both show a ratio of 1 to 2”)
A reason offered for every option (WODB) or both columns full (SBD)
Disagreement resolved with reasoning
The mathematical idea named by students

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Vague answers (“they both have numbers”) left unchallenged
The hunt for the one “correct” odd-one-out (there isn’t one)
The teacher supplying all the comparisons
Rushing past it without naming the idea

blocks.title: The point isn’t the answer — it’s the justification

blocks.text: In WODB especially, students sometimes race to “find the right one.” Redirect: the question is *which could you defend, and with what mathematics?* The same holds for Same But Different — “they’re different” is empty until a student names the precise, mathematical difference.

items: **The lowest floor of the comparison routines** — every student can offer one “same,” one “different,” or one reason a figure doesn’t belong.
**No single right answer** removes the fear of being wrong — powerful for students with math anxiety, and WODB’s “everyone’s right for a reason” makes that explicit.
**Sentence stems** (“These are the same because…” / “___ doesn’t belong because…”) scaffold language for multilingual learners.
**Visual sets** (shapes, graphs, pictures) let students connect representations with a low reading load.

blocks.text: Free ready-made libraries exist for both — **samebutdifferentmath.com** and **wodb.ca**. Start with one your students will have strong opinions about; the debate is what fuels the talk.

blocks.text: An **Opener routine** — reach for it when your purpose is to surface **equivalence, connections between representations, or precise distinctions and properties**.
Pick the format by purpose

rows: **Same But Different** (a pair) — the two-column same/different makes it crisp.
**WODB** (a set of four) — the “everyone’s right for a reason” set drives argument.
Maximize **participation & debate** early in building discourse
**WODB** — every student can defend at least one option.
Build **precise comparative language** (“same value, different form”)

blocks.text: Same But Different — choosing a pair (6–8)
The lever is the pair: pick two objects whose *“same”* is the idea you want surfaced and whose *“different”* is worth naming precisely.
Press for precision: “Same *how*? What do we *call* that?” The follow-up is where the mathematics gets made.
WODB — building a good set (the secret)
A strong WODB set has **a defensible reason for each of the four**. You don’t need every reason to be airtight — just arguable. Build it so different students will pick different ones.

items: **Choose four items** sharing a theme (four numbers, four graphs, four fractions).
**Make sure each can be “the odd one”** for a different property — one is the only even, one the only non-square, one the only single-digit, etc.
**Plan the math you want named** behind each likely reason.

blocks.text: Worked WODB examples (6–8)

rows: `3/8` — the only one not equal to 1/2 (value); `0.5` — only decimal; `2/4` — only one not in lowest terms; `1/2` — the simplest fraction form.
`16` — only even; `43` — only non-perfect-square (and only prime); `9` — only single digit; `25` — only multiple of 5.
**Proportional vs not:** four graphs (some through origin, some not; some linear, one curved)
Each “doesn’t belong” for steepness, whether it passes through the origin (proportional), linear vs. non-linear, or increasing vs. decreasing — surfaces what makes a relationship proportional.

blocks.text: For WODB, collect a reason for *all four* before celebrating — the magic dies if you stop at the first “right” answer. For Same But Different, gather several “sames” and “differents” before pressing for precision, so participation is wide before it goes deep.

items: **Everyone contributes one observation** — collect broadly before pressing, so every student is in before the reasoning deepens.
**Two-column (SBD) or four-quadrant (WODB) structure** gives a visual anchor that supports memory and language.
**Use a visual set** when you want to lower the reading load while keeping the mathematics rigorous.

blocks.text: Where this leads

Comparing and justifying is the heart of **Connecting Representations** in Core Instruction. These two openers build the habit — and the precise language — that students lean on when they justify and connect strategies during a task consolidation.
